Sir
SUR
n.
From Old French sire, from Latin senior, elder. Webster 1828: a word of respect used in addresses to men. In the Gospels it renders the Greek kurios in its ordinary courteous sense — the same word that elsewhere means Lord, and the gap between the two is often the point.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Greeks at the feast approach an apostle with a request that has been the text of a thousand pulpit fronts: The same came therefore to Philip, which was of Bethsaida of Galilee, and desired him, saying, Sir, we would see Jesus (John 12:21). They address Philip courteously and ask for the only thing worth asking. The Samaritan woman uses the same word to a stranger at a well and does not yet know what she is saying: Sir, thou hast nothing to draw with, and the well is deep: from whence then hast thou that living water? (John 4:11) — by the end of the chapter the courtesy has become confession. The Philippian jailor’s question is the plainest in Scripture: Sirs, what must I do to be saved? (Acts 16:30), and the answer given him is equally plain. John, overwhelmed in the Revelation, answers an elder’s question with a confession of ignorance that is also a submission: And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb (Revelation 7:14).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SIR as a word of respect used in addresses to men, as Madam is to women; also the title of a knight or baronet; and in the plural, a mode of address to a company of men.

expand to see more

SIR, n. — A word of respect used in addresses to men, as Madam is in addresses to women.

The title of a knight or baronet; as Sir Isaac Newton.

In the plural, SIRS, a mode of addressing a company of men.

Formerly a title of respect given to priests and to graduates of universities.

Old French sire, from Latin senior, elder — the same root as senator and senior.

Key Scripture

John 12:21 — "The same came therefore to Philip, which was of Bethsaida of Galilee, and desired him, saying, Sir, we would see Jesus."

John 4:11 — "The woman saith unto him, Sir, thou hast nothing to draw with, and the well is deep: from whence then hast thou that living water?"

Acts 16:30 — "And brought them out, and said, Sirs, what must I do to be saved?"

Revelation 7:14 — "And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb."

Modern Corruption

The jailor’s question and its answer are the New Testament’s plainest statement of the way of salvation, and both the question and the answer are routinely made more complicated than Scripture makes them.

expand to see more

Sirs, what must I do to be saved? is asked by a man who has just felt an earthquake and drawn his sword on himself, and the apostolic answer is Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house (Acts 16:31). Nothing is added as a condition — no penance, no probation, no rite performed first. Rome’s sacramental system makes baptism the instrument of regeneration and adds the whole apparatus of merit and satisfaction; the answer to the jailor knows nothing of it. But the passage equally refuses the reduction that treats belief as bare assent, for the narrative goes straight on to the washing of the apostles’ stripes, the household’s baptism, and rejoicing — faith immediately producing what faith produces. Believing on the Lord Jesus Christ is trust in a Person, and the fruit follows in the same paragraph.

John 4:11 rewards attention to the single Greek word. Kurios can mean nothing more than sir, and that is all the woman means at the well; by John 4:19 she calls Him a prophet, and by 4:29 she is asking whether this is the Christ. The Authorized Version’s rendering preserves the distance she still has to travel, and it is a useful corrective to the assumption that a person’s first words about Christ measure his final estimate of Him. Conversion in Scripture is often a lengthening of a title. It is also worth noting who receives this fullest self-disclosure of Messiah in the Gospels — a Samaritan woman with five husbands — which is the sovereign freedom of grace exercised exactly where respectable religion would not have looked.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kurios (G2962), lord, master, sir; despotes (G1203), master or sovereign; Latin senior, elder, the source of the English word.

expand to see more

Greek kurios (G2962) — lord, master, and in ordinary courtesy sir; the same word rendered Lord of Christ throughout the New Testament.

Greek aner (G435) — a man; in the vocative plural it gives the jailor’s Sirs (Acts 16:30).

Greek despotes (G1203) — a master with absolute authority, used of God in Luke 2:29 and Acts 4:24.

Greek pisteuo (G4100) — to believe, to trust; the whole of the apostolic answer (Acts 16:31).

Latin senior — elder; through Old French sire into English sir.

Usage

"Sir, we would see Jesus (John 12:21) — courteous address, and the only request worth making."

"Sirs, what must I do to be saved? (Acts 16:30) — the plainest question in Scripture, and the plainest answer."

"Sir, thou knowest (Revelation 7:14) — a confession of ignorance that is also a submission."
